entry.title: 🎭 What does the future of opera sound like?

media:group.media:title: 🎭 What does the future of opera sound like?
media:group.media:description:
For more than 200 years, audiences have filled Munich's National Theatre to experience world-class performances. Today, we're using digital twin technology to bring that experience far beyond its physical walls.
Together with the Bayerische Staatsoper, we've created a digital twin of the iconic venue that captures one of its most important characteristics: its acoustics. By combining real-world data, physics, and acoustic simulation, we've created an immersive mixed reality experience that lets users hear how performances will sound before a single note is played.
Musicians, conductors, planners, and opera lovers can explore the venue in entirely new ways and experience the sound of Munich's National Theatre from anywhere.
As Cedrik Neike puts it: digital twins can help bring the opera house to everybody.

entry.title: How do people develop at Siemens? | Growing Together - Episode 2

media:group.media:title: How do people develop at Siemens? | Growing Together - Episode 2
media:group.media:description:
In this honest, podcast-style conversation, six colleagues from Siemens in Germany talk openly about growing through challenges at work — from redefining failure and owning up to mistakes, to building trust, autonomy, and a genuine support network on the job. It's a candid look at what working at Siemens is really like, for anyone considering a career in engineering, digitalization, cybersecurity, product management, or UX research.
Explore career opportunities at Siemens Germany: https://sie.ag/4w3gVW
The discussion starts with a familiar idea in workplace culture: "celebrate failure." Rather than taking that at face value, the group unpacks what it actually means — separating simple mistakes from real failure, discussing why psychological safety depends on leaders modeling openness about their own setbacks, and reframing the conversation around embracing challenges instead of chasing a perfect record.
From there, the conversation moves into what keeps people motivated and supported day to day: caring for colleagues beyond the task at hand, staying connected across distributed and hybrid teams (including lessons learned during the pandemic), and having a network of managers and teammates you can rely on. The group also talks candidly about autonomy — having room to make decisions, take ownership, and learn by doing — and what personally keeps each of them engaged, from strong team relationships to working alongside colleagues who are genuinely passionate about their products.
The conversation features:
Velia Janetzky, Factory Digitalization, Erlangen Dr. Bahram Hamraz, Head of OT Protection & Consulting, Cybersecurity Mirko Menden, Customer Centric Innovation Mareike Weber, Product Owner, SIMATIC AX Dagmara Kukawka, Principal User Researcher Hosted by Lisa Sander
Whether you're early in your career or weighing your next move, this conversation offers an unscripted view into how Siemens people actually think about failure, growth, and what makes a workplace worth staying in.

entry.title: Recycling a High-Speed Train Into Raw Material for New Trains

media:group.media:title: Recycling a High-Speed Train Into Raw Material for New Trains
media:group.media:description:
This video follows Train2Train, a circular economy pilot led by Siemens Mobility that recovers aluminium from a decommissioned high-speed train and turns it into raw material for new rail vehicles. It is relevant for rail industry professionals, materials engineers, and sustainability specialists interested in circularity for the rail sector.
After roughly 30 years in service, a high-speed train reaches the end of its operating life. The Train2Train pilot uses it as the starting point for a closed material loop, addressing two challenges: capturing the end-of-life value of a train, and strengthening supply chain resilience for critical raw materials.
The video follows the material through the recycling process: shredding and fragmentation, air classification and magnetic separation into ferrous, non-ferrous, and plastic fractions, sorting of pre-shredded aluminium from a yard in Duisburg into alloy groups, and quality checks through drying, melting, and spark analysis to confirm the chemistry of the recovered metal.
Contributors describe why this matters: turning recovered aluminium into material that meets the quality demands of safety-relevant structural rail parts, and using a closed-loop approach to reduce dependence on primary raw materials. The video closes on what circularity means for the next generation of trains, built from material recovered from a decades-old vehicle.

entry.title: How Siemens Tech Keeps the Off-Grid Monte Rosa Hut Running

media:group.media:title: How Siemens Tech Keeps the Off-Grid Monte Rosa Hut Running
media:group.media:description:
At 2,883 meters in the Swiss Alps, the Monte Rosa Hut runs without a connection to the public power grid, making it one of the most advanced smart, autonomous buildings in the world. This video is for facility managers, building owners, and sustainability professionals who want to see how Siemens building management and digital platform technology operate in one of the most extreme real-world environments.
Learn more about the project: https://sie.ag/4j2Tf7
Fabian Gerschwiler, a Business Development Professional for digital platforms at Siemens Switzerland, walks through what keeps the hut running behind its striking facade. At the center of the building is Desigo CC, the Siemens building management system that connects photovoltaics, battery storage, heating, ventilation, and water treatment into a single system.
The hut generates most of its electricity from 84 square meters of photovoltaic panels integrated into its south-facing facade and installed on the surrounding rocks. Because solar output varies throughout the day, that electricity is stored in a battery system of 14 lithium-iron-phosphate batteries with a combined capacity of 215 kilowatt hours, enough to keep the hut running for up to three days with little or no sunshine. A backup diesel generator covers any longer gap in solar production.
Heating relies on a field of thermal solar collectors that capture heat for hot water and space heating, while a heat-recovery ventilation system reuses energy from outgoing air. Meltwater from the surrounding glacier is treated and disinfected before use, and greywater is treated and reused to reduce overall water consumption.
The video also shows how the hut is managed when nobody can reach it. Since 2024, the Siemens digital building platform Building X has connected to Desigo CC, sending building data to the cloud so its Energy Manager and Operations Manager applications can monitor energy flows, detect inefficiencies, and support remote troubleshooting from anywhere in the world. This is what allows the hut to keep operating safely through the winter, when heavy snow makes it inaccessible and even the hut wardens leave the site.
Together, these systems show what it takes to run a comfortable, resource-efficient building in one of the most demanding locations on earth.

entry.title: How is it to join Siemens? | Growing Together - Episode 1

media:group.media:title: How is it to join Siemens? | Growing Together - Episode 1
media:group.media:description:
What does it actually take to build a career at Siemens? In this episode, host Lisa Sander talks with colleagues from Siemens in Germany about how their individual career paths came together, and how they ended up working with one another.
Explore current opportunities at Siemens Germany: https://sie.ag/5VHpi1
Episode one of Growing Together brings together colleagues from across Siemens: Mirko Menden (Customer Centric Innovation), Dr. Bahram Hamraz (Head of OT Protection & Consulting), Velia Janetzky (Factory Digitalization, Erlangen), Mareike Weber (Product Owner, SIMATIC AX), and Dagmara Kukawka (Principal User Researcher). Together, they share their perspectives throughout the conversation.
Mirko explains how the Siemens Graduate Program, a two-year rotational program with three assignments across different parts of the company, became the starting point for several of the connections in the group. He traces how graduate community meetups and a factory visit in Erlangen turned into long-term working relationships.
Bahram shares a different kind of path. He once planned to study medicine like his father before switching to industrial engineering, completing a PhD in systems architecture, and eventually moving into cybersecurity about a year and a half ago. He speaks candidly about what it took to shift from a technical engineering role into leading OT cybersecurity, and why the learning curve in that field never really ends.
The group also discusses career planning itself. Mirko recalls being asked to sketch out a "mountain model" career plan early in his time at Siemens, only to end up not following it at all, with new opportunities instead arriving through conversations and chance connections over the years. His advice for anyone considering Siemens: rather than fixing on one job title, get clear on the topics, people, and environment you want to work in. With Siemens' breadth of businesses, the right fit is usually out there.
This conversation is relevant to job seekers, recent graduates, and career changers curious about what working at Siemens looks like day to day, including how internal mobility, networking, and less linear paths can shape a long-term career.

entry.title: Pergamon Altar Digital: Gods and Giants in Photorealistic 3D

media:group.media:title: Pergamon Altar Digital: Gods and Giants in Photorealistic 3D
media:group.media:description:
The gods and giants of the Gigantomachy — carved into the Pergamon Altar's Great Frieze — have been out of public view for years. Through Pergamon Altar Digital, a joint project by the Siemens Arts Program and Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz, SPK), the frieze is being recreated in photorealistic digital detail.
No tickets. No opening hours. No borders. Once the web version launches, anyone, anywhere will be able to explore one of antiquity's most dramatic sculptures, long before the Pergamon Museum reopens its doors on June 4, 2027.
Stay tuned.

media:group.media:description:
Diego joined Siemens in 1991. Sofía wasn't born yet.

They are both learning from each other. Neither treats the age gap as a hierarchy. Sofía brings new ideas and a habit of thinking outside the box. Diego brings decades of experience and knowledge, built up over time. Together, they call the mix "the power."
We believe growth doesn't move in one direction. It moves both ways, across career stages, every day.
